verdict: OK to lend in Hubballi-Dharwad engineering and capital goods, but only to component and machining SMEs with real order visibility and a working-capital cycle we can see; avoid pure EPC and single-buyer shops.
title: Hubballi-Dharwad Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative: Pricing power is thin on standard parts and real only where the firm holds a drawing and a qualification the buyer cannot quickly replicate. Capex is lumpy (a machining centre or a casting line), so utilisation and order cover decide whether the loan services itself.

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is genuinely strong: India-wide IIP for NIC 28 output is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date [D], and Karnataka's electricity demand is +23.3% Apr-to-date against India's +9.5% [D].** Karnataka GST collections are +11.1% Apr-to-date versus India's +6.1% [D], so the state's own consumption and investment are running ahead. The Rs 5 lakh crore Karnataka urbanisation plan, with 80% of investment front-loaded by 2032, names industrial clusters, roads and rail [1] — that is order flow for fabrication and T&D suppliers, not for us to lend against yet. Local coverage is thin: the ET Hubballi-Dharwad project page [2] carries no usable project detail, so treat city-level order news as unverified until you see the purchase order.

## Where the growth is — and who to avoid
**Pursue tier-2 machining and casting suppliers with two or more OEM buyers, railway and power T&D fabricators, and firms feeding the HDB cluster's engineering-services and aerospace/defence centres [3].** The HDB region now has more than 150 technology companies and around 10-plus VLSI firms [3], and peers confirm the pull: Skipper posted its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% [6], DEE's order book crossed Rs 1,300 crore with Q3 revenue up 77% [5], and Pitti is commissioning a Hyderabad casting and machining plant backed by order visibility from data centres, mining and railways [4]. Avoid single-customer job shops, pure EPC bidders dependent on bank guarantees for tenders [9], and anyone whose growth is volume without margin — Suzlon grew revenue 26% but EBITDA margin fell to 14.8% from 18.6% [7].

## How to grow safely
**Structure every limit around the cash conversion cycle, because EPC cash cycles run longer than OEMs' [11] and a growth-phase borrower with a short cycle needs less incremental working capital [8].** So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days by buyer and the inventory held for a single order; if receivables exceed the stated credit terms, ask for the buyer's payment ledger and the last three months' bank statements. Take monthly: stock-and-debtor statement, order book with buyer names and delivery dates, GST returns, and electricity bills to confirm the plant is actually running. Sanction as a cash-credit limit with a drawing power against current assets, not a term loan for capacity the order book does not cover.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for receivable days stretching while sales stay flat, inventory building against a cancelled or delayed order, and a customer concentration crossing half of turnover.** If a borrower's largest buyer delays payment by one cycle, cut drawing power immediately and ask for the buyer's confirmation of outstanding. If electricity consumption falls while invoices rise, stop fresh disbursement and inspect the plant. If a term loan is being used to fund working capital, restructure to cash credit before the next quarter.
